narrative.note: Jordan, this is Riley's very first progress report, so think of it as a starting line, not a scoreboard. Every subject here is a fresh starting point, and that's completely normal for a first look. Since Riley loves trucks, there are easy ways to bring that love into counting, sorting, and storytelling this month. Reading is exactly where I'd start, too, and I've got a clear next step below.

subjects.math: Counting five objects one at a time is the next thing to watch for, and touching each item while counting out loud (crackers, toy trucks, stairs) makes it click.
subjects.literacy: Riley isn't yet recognizing the letters in their own name, which is a wonderful first goal since a name is the most personal word there is.
subjects.phonics: Clapping out the beats in a word, like ba-na-na, is the next small step, and it turns into a game anywhere you have a spare minute.
subjects.writing: Right now the next step is holding a crayon with fingers instead of a fist, and playful drawing time builds that grip naturally.
subjects.language: Telling you about something that happened earlier today is next on the list, and a simple 'tell me about the park' after fun moments helps that story come out.
subjects.science: Sorting things into groups, like big versus small, is the next step, and everyday objects around the house are all you need to practice.
subjects.social_studies: Naming family members and how they connect, like grandma being mommy's mom, is the next thing to watch for, and it often comes out naturally in conversation.
subjects.art: Naming the main colors while drawing or painting is next, and pointing out colors during art time is a gentle, built-in way to practice.
subjects.music: Clapping or tapping along to a steady beat is the next step, and simple copy-the-clap games are a fun, quick way to build that.
subjects.gross_motor: Galloping with one foot leading the other is next on the list, and silly animal-walk races are a great way to build that coordination.
subjects.fine_motor: Stringing large beads or threading laces is the next step, and scissors practice with paper strips builds the same hand strength along the way.
subjects.social_emotional: Playing WITH other kids, taking turns and sharing with reminders, is the next step, and lots of practice moments will come naturally through play.
subjects.self_care: Using the toilet during the day with only occasional misses is next, and turning routines like buttoning into a game can help build related skills.
subjects.executive_function: Waiting a short turn without falling apart, even with support, is the next step, and games like freeze dance make that practice feel like fun instead of a test.
subjects.computer_science: This one is all about exposure, so whenever you like, playing 'robot' together, giving each other step-by-step instructions, is a fun way to explore this.
subjects.spanish: There's no rush here at all, it's about exposure when it fits your family, and picking one everyday word to use all week is a light, low-pressure way to start.

narrative.synthesis: Riley is right at the start of so many exciting first steps, and that's exactly where a four-year-old should be. Notice how many of these threads connect: naming colors while drawing, sorting by size, and noticing family connections are all the same kind of noticing skill, just pointed in different directions. Telling you about their day and clapping out word beats are both early forms of the same thing, putting sounds and stories into shape. Since Riley loves trucks, you can lean into that everywhere: count the wheels, sort trucks by size, gallop like a truck racing down the hall. If you're looking for the single best place to focus this month, reading is a great one to start with, since letter recognition and clapping out word beats both feed directly into it. Small, playful moments repeated often will do more than any big sit-down lesson, and you clearly already know how to make learning feel like play.

drawers.math: When asked, Riley wasn't yet counting five objects one at a time and saying how many there are, which is typically seen by four years old. This isn't a race, it just tells us where to point next. Touching each object while counting out loud, one more than the day before, builds this skill naturally over time.
drawers.literacy: Riley isn't yet recognizing the letters in their own name, a skill often seen by three and a half. Their name is the most meaningful word in the world to them, so hunting for its letters on signs, boxes, and books turns practice into a game.

drawers.writing: Riley isn't yet holding a crayon with fingers instead of a fist, typically seen by four. Grip strength grows through play, not drills, so big, colorful name-tracing activities help build the hand muscles behind a comfortable pencil grip.
drawers.language: Telling you about something that happened earlier in the day isn't happening yet, typically seen by four. Prompting Riley to retell a fun moment, like what happened at the park, gives them practice putting events into words with you there to help.
drawers.science: Sorting things into groups, like big versus small or animals versus plants, isn't happening yet, typically seen by three years eight months. Simple sorting games with everyday objects, like guessing which small items will sink or float, build this thinking skill through play.
drawers.social_studies: Naming family members and how they connect isn't happening yet, typically seen by three years ten months. Drawing a simple map of home together and marking where everyone sleeps is a playful way to talk through who's who in the family.
drawers.art: Naming the main colors while drawing or painting isn't happening yet, typically seen by three and a half. Pairing color words with hands-on art, like drawing along to music, helps those color names stick through repetition.
drawers.music: Clapping or tapping along to a steady beat isn't happening yet, typically seen right around now, four years two months. Simple copy-the-pattern clapping games, taking turns leading, build this rhythm sense quickly and playfully.
drawers.gross_motor: Galloping with one foot leading isn't happening yet, typically seen by four. Playful animal-walk races down the hallway build coordination and are an easy daily movement break.
drawers.fine_motor: Stringing large beads or threading laces isn't happening yet, typically seen right around now, four years two months. Scissor practice, snipping paper into confetti, builds the same hand strength and control needed for beading.
drawers.social_emotional: Playing WITH other kids, taking turns and sharing with reminders, isn't happening yet, typically seen right around now. Naming big feelings out loud in the moment, then offering two simple choices, helps build the self-control that turn-taking needs.
drawers.self_care: Using the toilet during the day with only occasional misses isn't happening yet, typically seen by four. This is a big milestone that comes in its own time, and turning related routines, like buttoning clothes, into a game keeps things light along the way.

drawers.spanish: This is an exposure area, so it's entirely about what your family chooses to explore, whenever that feels right. Picking one useful word or phrase and using it naturally all week, at meals or during play, is a low-pressure way to start.

narrative.keepsake: Riley, right now you are four years old and full of energy for trucks, the kind of love that makes every wheel and engine sound exciting. Jordan has been watching closely to see all the new things you're learning to do, from counting to drawing to telling stories about your day. You're the kind of person who notices the world around you and wants to be part of everything happening in it. There is so much ahead for you to discover, one small step at a time, and every bit of it is worth celebrating. With love, Homa.
